Several years ago Daewoo Shipbuilding and Marine Engineering (DSME) and Netherlands Maritime Technology (NMT) began researching renewable methods of ship propulsion. The methods that won out and advanced to the prototype stage were wind and solar. Nuclear options are still being investigated, but still need to account for all of the security concerns and finalize reactor designs.

The primary method takes it's inspiration from one of the oldest methods of ship propulsion, the sail. Large retractable sails are installed along the top of the ship and controlled to take advantage of the abundant wind power in order to save fuel. The sails can retract when not needed or during bad weather and can be rotated to optimally catch crosswinds. Navigation systems have also been designed that can guide the ships along optimized paths that take advantage of winds and avoid harsh weather.

In addition solar panels can be installed on the top of certain types of ships, such as tankers and bulk carriers, that will charge Li-ion batteries to power other electrical systems on the ship. The design includes an automatic switching system to charge the batteries from the solar panels only when they are generating current, which would otherwise come from the traditional power plants that remain in the ship.

The Dutch company, DAMEN Shipyards Gorinchem, have been working on their own LeanShips technologies that will be utilized in these new ships. These technologies provide cleaner, lower emission liquid natural gas drives.

The combination of these technologies with the sails and solar panels are expected to provide fuel savings of at least 35%. The Netherlands and South Korea specified a recently completed Valemax Bulk Carrier to install and test these technologies on. A new container ship design was also built to accomodate the sail system, but won't be accommodating the solar panels. Trials have taken place over the last year to test these technologies in action.

Trials found a savings of 35% for the ships that can accommodate solar panels and 32% for ships that cannot. Engineers suspect that greater savings may be realized after the first wave of production ships are evaluated. DAMEN Engineers also found some malfunctions with their LeanShips LNG drives that are being fine tuned.
